content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections predominantly occur in healthcare environments. Proper hand hygiene and adherence to infection prevention protocols are essential to minimize the risk of infection. This bacterium is often resistant to antibiotics, which makes treating these infections particularly challenging. Pseudomonas is a genus of bacteria commonly found in natural environments such as soil and water. Among these, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most frequent cause of infections in humans. It can lead to infections in the bloodstream, lungs (resulting in pneumonia), urinary tract, or other areas of the body, particularly following surgical procedures. Certain strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa are resistant to nearly all available antibiotics, including carbapenems, and are classified as multidrug-resistant (MDR) Pseudomonas aeruginosa. In 2017, MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa was responsible for an estimated 32,600 infections in hospitalized patients and approximately 2,700 deaths in the United States. Individuals at the highest risk for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections are those in healthcare settings, particularly patients who are on mechanical ventilators, have indwelling medical devices such as catheters, or have open wounds from surgery or burns. The bacterium can spread through contact with contaminated surfaces or medical equipment, exposure to contaminated soil or water, or person-to-person transmission, such as through unclean hands. To reduce the risk of infection, patients and caregivers should maintain proper hand hygiene, especially before and after wound care or handling medical devices. They should also remind healthcare providers to clean their hands before patient contact or device handling. In healthcare settings, patients should allow staff to clean their rooms daily. Healthcare providers and facilities must adhere to core infection control practices to prevent the spread of these bacteria and should implement water management plans to minimize exposure risks. To diagnose a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, healthcare providers collect a specimen and send it to a laboratory for antimicrobial susceptibility testing. This testing identifies the most effective treatment options. Treatment for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections typically involves antibiotics. However, treatment options are limited for multidrug-resistant strains, complicating recovery. The CDC is actively addressing Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections by providing testing to identify cases of antimicrobial resistance, measuring resistance patterns, and tracking transmission within healthcare settings through the Antimicrobial Resistance Laboratory Network. The CDC also monitors these infections via the National Healthcare Safety Network, with data accessible through the AR & Patient Safety Portal. Additionally, the CDC collaborates with health departments, federal agencies, healthcare providers, and patients to prevent Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections and curb the spread of resistant strains.
